# Glossary of 2020s slang

Glossary of 2020s slang

"Glossary of Generation Z slang" and "Glossary of Generation Alpha slang" redirect here. For youth slang in general, see [Youth slang](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Youth_slang "Youth slang").

English-language slang used or popularized in the 2020s, usually by [Generation Z](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Generation_Z "Generation Z") (Gen Z) or by [Generation Alpha](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Generation_Alpha "Generation Alpha") (Gen Alpha), differs from that of earlier generations.[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glossary_of_2020s_slang#cite_note-1)[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glossary_of_2020s_slang#cite_note-ft-2) Ease of communication via social media and other internet outlets has facilitated its rapid proliferation, creating "an unprecedented variety of linguistic variation", according to Danielle Abril of _[The Washington Post](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Washington_Post "The Washington Post")_.[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glossary_of_2020s_slang#cite_note-ft-2)[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glossary_of_2020s_slang#cite_note-CS-3)[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glossary_of_2020s_slang#cite_note-4) [Self-deprecating](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Self-deprecation "Self-deprecation") irony is often a prevalent factor in its use.

Many Gen Z and Gen Alpha slang terms were not originally coined by their generation but were already in use or simply became more mainstream. Much of what is considered Gen Z and Gen Alpha slang originates from [African-American Vernacular English](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/African-American_Vernacular_English "African-American Vernacular English"), [Black queer ball culture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ball_culture "Ball culture"), and [incel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Incel "Incel") culture.[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glossary_of_2020s_slang#cite_note-ft-2)[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glossary_of_2020s_slang#cite_note-5)[\[6\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glossary_of_2020s_slang#cite_note-6)[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glossary_of_2020s_slang#cite_note-7)

This is a [dynamic list](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:WikiProject_Lists#Dynamic_lists "Wikipedia:WikiProject Lists") and may never be able to satisfy particular standards for completeness. You can help by [editing the page](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Special:EditPage/Glossary_of_2020s_slang "Special:EditPage/Glossary of 2020s slang") to add missing items, with references to [reliable sources](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Reliable_sources "Wikipedia:Reliable sources").

## A

| Term | Definition | References |
| --- | --- | --- |
| acoustic/artistic | [Algospeak](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algospeak "Algospeak") forms of the word " [autistic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Autistic "Autistic")." Used as insults to call someone stupid, in the same manner as " [retarded](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Retard_(pejorative) "Retard (pejorative)")" has come to be used. | [\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glossary_of_2020s_slang#cite_note-8) |
| [and I oop](https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/and%20I%20oop "wikt:and I oop") | Used to express shock, embarrassment, and/or amusement. Often associated with [VSCO girls](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/VSCO_girl "VSCO girl") alongside ' [sksksk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glossary_of_2020s_slang#S)'. | [\[9\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glossary_of_2020s_slang#cite_note-9)[\[10\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glossary_of_2020s_slang#cite_note-independent-10) |
| aura | An individual's current reputation or charisma. Cultivating aura is known as [aura farming](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aura_farming "Aura farming"). | [\[11\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glossary_of_2020s_slang#cite_note-11) |
| ate | To have performed well or extremely good at something. | [\[12\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glossary_of_2020s_slang#cite_note-12) |

## B

| Term | Definition | References |
| --- | --- | --- |
| baddie | A confident, stylish, and attractive woman or girl. | [\[13\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glossary_of_2020s_slang#cite_note-13) |
| ball knowledge | niche or uncommon knowledge, usually niche references, often in pop culture. Alternative forms include "elite ball knowledge" or "knowing ball". | [\[14\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glossary_of_2020s_slang#cite_note-14) |
| based | Originated from rapper [Lil B The BasedGod](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lil_B "Lil B"), who defined it as "...being yourself. Not being scared of what people think about you. Not being afraid to do what you wanna do." More contemporary use has been to express approval of someone or agreeing with another's opinion, similar to the usage of " [W](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glossary_of_2020s_slang#W)". The term is often used by the [alt-right](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alt-right "Alt-right"). | [\[15\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glossary_of_2020s_slang#cite_note-15)[\[16\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glossary_of_2020s_slang#cite_note-BASED-KQED-16)[\[17\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glossary_of_2020s_slang#cite_note-17)[\[18\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glossary_of_2020s_slang#cite_note-18) |
| [basic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Basic_(slang) "Basic (slang)") | those who prefer mainstream products, trends, and music. Derived from the term " [basic bitch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Basic_bitch "Basic bitch")". | [\[19\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glossary_of_2020s_slang#cite_note-19)[\[20\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glossary_of_2020s_slang#cite_note-20)[\[21\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glossary_of_2020s_slang#cite_note-UK-21) |
| bar(s) | A lyric in a [rap](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rap "Rap") song that is considered excellent. A talented rapper may be said to "drop bars" or be "spitting bars", sometimes shortened to just "spitting". | [\[22\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glossary_of_2020s_slang#cite_note-22) |
| BDE | Abbreviation for " [big dick energy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Big_dick_energy "Big dick energy")": confidence and ease. | [\[23\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glossary_of_2020s_slang#cite_note-23) |
| Bean Soup Theory | A specific phenomenon described as a 'What about me' effect. An individual watches a video that doesn't pertain to them, but finds a way to make it about them anyway. Stems from a 2023 TikTok recipe for bean soup by @vibingranolamom with commenters saying "What if I don't like beans?" | [\[24\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glossary_of_2020s_slang#cite_note-24) |
| beige flag | A behavior or personality trait that is neither good nor bad. Derived from the relationship terms " [green flag](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Green_flag "Green flag")" and " [red flag](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_flag_(idiom) "Red flag (idiom)")". | [\[25\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glossary_of_2020s_slang#cite_note-RG-25) |
| bet | Agreeing to something; yes; okay; sure. | [\[26\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glossary_of_2020s_slang#cite_note-26) |
| bffr | Acronym for "be fucking for real". | [\[27\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glossary_of_2020s_slang#cite_note-27) |
| big back | an overweight and gluttonous person. | [\[28\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glossary_of_2020s_slang#cite_note-28) |
| big yikes | something embarrassing or cringeworthy, particularly in response to an offensive comment. | [\[29\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glossary_of_2020s_slang#cite_note-29) |
| big yahu | Nickname for [Israeli Prime Minister](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Israeli_Prime_Minister "Israeli Prime Minister") [Benjamin Netanyahu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Benjamin_Netanyahu "Benjamin Netanyahu"), sometimes used to portray Netanyahu as a spiritual being who assists in minor inconveniences. | [\[30\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glossary_of_2020s_slang#cite_note-30) |
| bop | (1) A [derogatory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pejorative "Pejorative") term, usually for females, suggesting excessive flirtatiousness or promiscuity. (2) An exceptionally good song. (3) An acronym for "baddie on point", meaning someone who uses their appearance to make money. | (1)[\[31\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glossary_of_2020s_slang#cite_note-31) (2)[\[32\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glossary_of_2020s_slang#cite_note-32)[\[33\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glossary_of_2020s_slang#cite_note-33) (3)[\[34\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glossary_of_2020s_slang#cite_note-34) |
| [brain rot](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brain_rot "Brain rot") (or brainrot) | The state of being detached from the real world as a result of consuming [hyper-stimulating](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stimulation "Stimulation") or [chronically online](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chronically_online "Chronically online") content, especially when characterized by online buzzwords (e.g., " [skibidi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Skibidi_Toilet "Skibidi Toilet")", " [fanum tax](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fanum_tax "Fanum tax")", " [rizz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rizz "Rizz")", etc). Derived from the idea that one's brain would "rot" from consuming too much stimulating, addictive or degenerate content. | [\[35\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glossary_of_2020s_slang#cite_note-35)[\[36\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glossary_of_2020s_slang#cite_note-36)[\[37\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glossary_of_2020s_slang#cite_note-37) |
| [bruh/bru](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bro_culture "Bro culture") ([/brʌ/](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:IPA/English "Help:IPA/English")[Play audio](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/transcoded/1/16/En-us-bruh-noun.ogg/En-us-bruh-noun.ogg.mp3 "Play audio")[ⓘ](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:En-us-bruh-noun.ogg "File:En-us-bruh-noun.ogg")) | A variant of "bro" originating in the 1800's, becoming more popular in 1967, again in 2003. Bruh resurged once more in the late 2010s, entering heavy use in [Gen Z](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gen_Z "Gen Z") & [Gen Alpha](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gen_Alpha "Gen Alpha") slang. | [\[38\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glossary_of_2020s_slang#cite_note-38)[\[39\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glossary_of_2020s_slang#cite_note-fm-39)[\[40\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glossary_of_2020s_slang#cite_note-40) |
| buns | Something that is considered bad or low quality. | [\[41\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glossary_of_2020s_slang#cite_note-41) |
| bussin' | Extremely good, excellent. Originated from African-American vernacular for delicious food. | [\[42\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glossary_of_2020s_slang#cite_note-42) |
| bussy | Portmanteau of "boy" and "pussy" (slang for the [vagina](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vagina "Vagina")). Effectively a man's [anus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Human_anus "Human anus"), especially when used in gay penetrative sex. | [\[43\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glossary_of_2020s_slang#cite_note-43) |
| blud | A variant of "blood brother", "mate" or sometimes "bro". | [\[44\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glossary_of_2020s_slang#cite_note-44) |

## C

| Term | Definition | References |
| --- | --- | --- |
| cap | To [lie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lie "Lie") originating from AAVE. The antonym, "no cap", is typically used after a statement to indicate [truthfulness](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Honesty "Honesty") or being genuine. | [\[45\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glossary_of_2020s_slang#cite_note-45)[\[46\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glossary_of_2020s_slang#cite_note-nc-46)[\[47\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glossary_of_2020s_slang#cite_note-47) |
| caught in 4K | Refers to someone being indisputably caught doing something wrong or incriminating on camera or with evidence to prove it, referencing [4K resolution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/4K_resolution "4K resolution"). | [\[48\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glossary_of_2020s_slang#cite_note-48) |
| chopped | Physically unattractive or unfavorable. | [\[49\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glossary_of_2020s_slang#cite_note-49) |
| [chud](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chud_(pejorative) "Chud (pejorative)") | Originally a pejorative term for someone on the [far-right](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Far-right_politics "Far-right politics"). Commonly used to mean a rude, unattractive, lazy, socially inept, or unintelligent person, often in self-deprecation. | [\[50\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glossary_of_2020s_slang#cite_note-50) |
| [clanker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clanker "Clanker") | [Slur](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pejorative "Pejorative") for robots, primarily used against [generative AI](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Generative_AI "Generative AI"). Originated from _[Star Wars](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Star_Wars "Star Wars")_ media. | [\[51\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glossary_of_2020s_slang#cite_note-51)[\[52\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glossary_of_2020s_slang#cite_note-52) |
| clapback | Swift and witty response to an insult or critique. | [\[53\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glossary_of_2020s_slang#cite_note-53) |
| cook (verb) | To "cook" is to perform or do well. Often used in the phrase "let him cook". | [\[54\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glossary_of_2020s_slang#cite_note-54)[\[55\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glossary_of_2020s_slang#cite_note-55) |
| cooked (adjective) | To "be cooked" is to be in trouble. | [\[56\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glossary_of_2020s_slang#cite_note-56) |
| coworker music | Generic or overrated music that one's coworker might listen to. Typical examples are [stomp clap](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stomp_clap "Stomp clap") music or [pop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Popular_music "Popular music") rock like the [Imagine Dragons](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Imagine_Dragons "Imagine Dragons"). It has also been adapted to "coworker memes" and "coworker opinions" similar to " [normie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Normie_(slang) "Normie (slang)")". | [\[57\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glossary_of_2020s_slang#cite_note-57)\[ _[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_\] |
| cracked (adjective) | To be skilled at something. |  |
| cracked (verb) | Often used in the phrases "getting cracked" or "cracking," means to have sex. | [\[58\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glossary_of_2020s_slang#cite_note-58) |
| crash out / crashout | To have a bout of rage or upset. Sometimes more generally used to refer to anger or strong displeasure. Originated in the African-American community, specifically in Louisiana with usage by rappers like [NBA YoungBoy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NBA_YoungBoy "NBA YoungBoy"), but became popular on TikTok in 2024. | [\[59\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glossary_of_2020s_slang#cite_note-59)[\[60\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glossary_of_2020s_slang#cite_note-60)[\[61\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glossary_of_2020s_slang#cite_note-61)[\[62\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glossary_of_2020s_slang#cite_note-62) |
| crine | Variant pronunciation/spelling of "crying," typically meaning crying & dying from laughter (equivalent to "dying of laughter" or "I'm crying"). Often used in phrases like "son I'm crine". | \[ _[bettersourceneeded](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Verifiability#Questionable_sources "Wikipedia:Verifiability")_\][\[63\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glossary_of_2020s_slang#cite_note-63) |

## D

| Term | Definition | References |
| --- | --- | --- |
| dead/ded | Humorous to such an extent as to "kill you". Laughter and death have been associated since Ancient Greece, where it is held that [Zeuxis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zeuxis_(painter) "Zeuxis (painter)") died from laughing at a portrait of an ugly woman he was painting. | [\[64\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glossary_of_2020s_slang#cite_note-64)[\[65\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glossary_of_2020s_slang#cite_note-65) |
| delusionship | A relationship in which someone holds unrealistic or overly idealistic beliefs. A person who holds such beliefs is considered " [delulu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Delulu "Delulu")". | [\[66\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glossary_of_2020s_slang#cite_note-66)[\[67\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glossary_of_2020s_slang#cite_note-67)[\[68\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glossary_of_2020s_slang#cite_note-68) |
| dih | Ironic [algospeak](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algospeak "Algospeak") for [dick](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Penis "Penis"). Usually used with the wilting rose emoji for comedic effect or a symbolic eggplant emoji. | [\[69\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glossary_of_2020s_slang#cite_note-69) |
| drip | Good-looking or trendy [high-class](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Upper_class "Upper class") fashion. | [\[70\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glossary_of_2020s_slang#cite_note-70) |

## E

| Term | Definition | References |
| --- | --- | --- |
| [edge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edging_(sexual_practice) "Edging (sexual practice)") | To maintain a high level of [sexual arousal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sexual_arousal "Sexual arousal") for an extended period without reaching climax ( [orgasm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orgasm "Orgasm")). Often used as a dysphemism for keeping something close to completion or a goal for an undue amount of time. | [\[71\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glossary_of_2020s_slang#cite_note-71) |

## F

| Term | Definition | References |
| --- | --- | --- |
| face card | An attractive face. Sometimes defined as never declining or [receding](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Receding_hairline "Receding hairline"). | [\[72\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glossary_of_2020s_slang#cite_note-72)[\[73\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glossary_of_2020s_slang#cite_note-73) |
| fah | An onomatopoeic internet catchphrase and viral [TikTok](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/TikTok "TikTok") sound effect that represents a loud, distorted, and vocalized scream of the word " [fuck](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fuck "Fuck")". It is heavily used in video editing as an audio exclamation point or impact marker to humorously signal a sudden failure, shock, or spiritual collapse. Also sometimes spelt "fahh." | [\[74\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glossary_of_2020s_slang#cite_note-Times_India_Fahhh-74) |
| [fanum tax](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fanum_tax "Fanum tax") | Theft of food between friends. Referring to the [Twitch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Twitch_(service) "Twitch (service)") streamer [Fanum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fanum_(streamer) "Fanum (streamer)") who took cookies from fellow streamer [Kai Cenat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kai_Cenat "Kai Cenat") as a "tax" during a livestream. | [\[75\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glossary_of_2020s_slang#cite_note-75) |
| fine shyt | A slang term and phonetic variation of "fine shit", used to describe a highly attractive or desirable person. The spelling pattern follows the mainstream 2020s -h suffix mutation trend. It is frequently abbreviated online as "fs". | [\[76\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glossary_of_2020s_slang#cite_note-InTheKnow_Slang-76) |
| finna | Term used meaning "I am going to" or "I am about to". The term has its roots in [African American Vernacular English](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/African-American_Vernacular_English "African-American Vernacular English"), where "fixing to" has been used to mean "getting ready to" since the 18th century. Often used interchangeably with " [gonna](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gonna "Gonna")". | [\[77\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glossary_of_2020s_slang#cite_note-77) |

# Gen Z & Teen Slang: A Parent’s Guide to 200+ Terms (2026)

By [Jackie Baucom](https://gabb.com/author/jackiebaucom/)

Share Article

November 6, 2026](https://gabb.com/blog/meet-the-safer-watch-for-kids-the-gabb-watch/)

**_Updated – Originally published January 17, 2024_**

As a parent, you’ve probably overheard some slang from your kid. They may say things like, “I’m amped about my drip today,” or “He’s got rizz. Giving off major BDE.”

Maybe they’ve said something like, “No cap, this sandwich is bussin’,” or “Spill the tea, sis!”

The [lingo our kids use](https://gabb.com/blog/emoji-meaning-chart/) every day may be incomprehensible to us, but these words actually have meaning—some we may know, and some we can understand from the context of the conversation.

A number of these slang terms were created by past generations, while others are new terms that parents can be pretty clueless about. Some of these words are made up, shortened, or said as acronyms. Some slang terms are everyday words but hold different meanings.

Many new terms stem organically from the online platforms kids commonly use to communicate today (which underscores the need for [safe tech](https://gabb.com/comparison-chart/), especially [when it comes to messaging](https://gabb.com/gabb-messenger/)).

We’ve come up with a list of popular slang words to help parents better understand their kids and their friends.

Teen slang is ALWAYS evolving, but our team will add more words as we collect them and slang trends emerge. So check back often!

![Gen Z Slang by Gabb](https://gabb.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/12/25-Teen-Slang-vertical-asset-1080x1920-1-576x1024-1.avif)

It’s important to note that slang terms can vary widely based on location, culture, and generation, and some may have different meanings or connotations depending on the context.

* * *

## _A-C_

* * *

[![Tech That Grows With Them](https://cdn.gabb.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/04/2026-MARCH-SALE-GW3e-GP4P-BLOG-1740x1020-1-600x352.png)](https://gabb.com/?utm_source=Blog&utm_medium=Blog&utm_campaign=inline&utm_content=homepageQ2ETIS)

### A

**Addy –** Abbreviation for Address.

_I’ll meet you there, just send me the_ **_addy_** _._

**AF –** An acronym that stands for As f\*\*k.

_I had the time of my life at the concert. It was lit_ **_AF_** _!_

**Amirite –** An informal way to say “am I right,” used to seek agreement after making a statement.

_That taco was bomb, **amirite?**_

**Amped –** Excited

_I’m_ **_amped_** _for the concert tonight!_

**And I oop –** Used to express surprise, shock, or realization, often in response to something unexpected or amusing.

_She accidentally knocked over her cup,_ **_and I oop_** _, there it goes all over the floor._

**ASL –** An abbreviation for “as hell.” It is used as an intensifier. This term may also be used as an acronym for “age, sex, location,” to quickly inquire about someone’s basic demographic information. But that usage has mostly been replaced by Gen Z with the new “as hell” usage.

_Those new shoes are cool **asl**._

**Ate and left no crumbs –** Refers to someone who did something so well that there’s no chance for anyone else to do it better.

_Did you see Emma’s floor routine? She_ **_ate and left no crumbs_** _!_

**Aura –** Like the traditional definition, it is used to compliment someone’s ability, perceived power, or sense of coolness and mystery. It became popular in soccer and basketball communities on Twitter in 2023 so it is often used to compliment athletes.

_Did you see Steph Curry’s clutch shot last night? He’s got crazy_ **_aura_** _._

**Aura points –** Imaginary points someone gains or loses for doing something cool or embarrassing. A humorous way to rate a person’s coolness in the moment.

_He tripped walking into class and lost major_ **_aura points_** _._

* * *

### B

**Bae –** Boyfriend or girlfriend.

_Wait,_ **_bae_** _is calling me._

**Bandwagon** – Someone who takes an interest in something just to fit in with the crowd.

_Maggie suddenly loves rugby, she is a major **bandwagon**_ fan.

**Basic –** Someone who is unoriginal and only interested in popular, trending things.

_She’s so_ **_basic_** _with her pumpkin spice latte._

**BBG –** An acronym that stands for baby girl, describing something or someone cute. It can also stand for: Better be going, a polite way to end a conversation.

_I love that dress on you_ **_bbg_** _!_

**_Bbg_** _, I have soccer practice._

**BDE –** An acronym that stands for: Big dick energy, someone who is secure and exudes confidence without arrogance.

_I knew she would get the internship—she has major_ **_BDE_** _!_

**Bed rot –** Spending extended periods of time in bed, often engaging in activities like watching TV or reading.

_After a hectic week, I’m looking forward to some much-needed_ **_bed rot_** _this weekend._

**Beige flag –** Used humorously to refer to a situation that is mundane, uninteresting, or lacking excitement.

_His alphabetized bookshelf is a_ **_beige flag._**

**Bet –** In agreement with something, or used for okay or affirmative.

Person 1: _Want to come over to my house?_

Person 2: **_Bet_** _!_

**Biblically accurate –** Describes something strange, overwhelming, or unsettling to look at, referencing depictions of “biblically accurate angels.” Usually used humorously.

_My little brother drew a_ **_biblically accurate_** _snowman and it’s kind of terrifying._

**Big back** – Refers to someone who is overweight, typically to bully or shame them.

_She ate that whole plate of spaghetti. That’s some **big back** behavior!_

**Big yikes** – A reaction to something very awkward, uncomfortable, or embarrassing.

_He tried to lie and got caught immediately — big yikes._

**Bih –** A phonetic spelling of “b\*\*\*h.” Often used in a less aggressive way, and depending on the tone and context, can be used jokingly among friends or as a playful term of endearment.

_She playfully teased her friend, calling her “_ **_bih_** _,” as they laughed together._

**Blueprint –** Someone who did something so well they became the standard everyone else copies.

_The way she styles those outfits — she’s the_ **_blueprint_** _._

**Body count –** The number of sexual partners someone has had.

_She was hesitant to reveal her_ **_body count_** _, fearing she’d be judged._

**Boo –** A term of endearment used to refer to a romantic partner.

_I can’t wait to see my_ **_boo_** _tonight._

**Boo’d up –** Refers to being in a romantic relationship with someone.

_After months of flirting, they finally_ **_boo’d up._**

**Boomer/Okay Boomer –** A dismissive retort used to mock the opinions, ideas, or attitudes of older individuals, particularly members of the Baby Boomer generation.

_When Clayton’s great-uncle started complaining about millennials’ work ethic, he responded with, “_ **_Okay, Boomer_** _.”_

**Boujee –** Rich, luxurious, fancy

_You grew up going to this_ **_boujee_** _country club?_

**Brat –** A term coined by singer Charlie XCX in a tweet, “brat” describes a person (often female) who is genuine, self-possessed, non-conforming, with a rebellious streak. It is represented by a florescent, chartreuse green, which symbolizes making a statement.

_Kamala is brat._

**Breadcrumbing –** Giving someone just enough occasional attention or flirty messages to keep them interested, with no intention of actually committing.

_He texts her once a week and then disappears. Classic_ **_breadcrumbing_** _._

**Bussin’** **–** Something is really good.

_This burrito is_ **_bussin’_** _! I’m definitely coming back here._

**Buttah** – A compliment that describes something that is smooth, easy, and good.

_That new song you dropped is pure **buttah**_.

* * *

### C

**Cake –** A large, well-shaped bottom.

_She caught him checking out her_ **_cake_** _as she walked past him at the beach._

**Cap –** Lying or faking.

_I actually went to class today. No_ **_cap_** _._

**Cash –** Awesome or cool.

_That new movie is so_ **_cash_** _!_

**Catch feels –** Develop romantic or emotional attachment to someone.

_I noticed Lea starting to_ **_catch feels_** _for Bruce._

**Catfish –** A person who creates a fake online persona to deceive others.

_He thought he was talking to a model on the dating app, but it turned out to be a_ **_catfish_** _using stolen photos from the internet._

**Caught in 4k –** Someone caught in the act of something compromising.

_He thought he could get away with lying, but we have him_ **_caught in 4k_** _._

**Chad**– A stereotypical, confident, dominant male. Often used humorously and with negative connotations.

_He thinks he knows everything. He’s such a **Chad**._

**Chat –** Used to refer to a group of people, like friends or people in their class.

**_Chat_** _, do you think he’s telling the truth?_

**Cheugy** – Someone or something that is out-of-date, unfashionable, or trying too hard.

_I can’t believe she’s still wearing skinny jeans, that’s so **cheugy**._

**Chopped –** Unattractive, low quality, or badly done.

_That haircut came out_ **_chopped_** _._

**Clapback –** A sharp and witty response to criticism or an insult.

_When Tori called her outfit cheugy, her_ **_clapback_** _was for real!_

**Clock/clocking –** To notice or call out something, especially something a person was trying to hide.

_She_ **_clocked_** _that he wasn’t telling the truth._

**Cooked –** Something or someone that is done, exhausted, or doomed.

_I was up all night but didn’t even get halfway through the study guide, I’m **cooked**._

**Core** **(Cottagecore, Barbiecore, etc.)**– A suffix used to describe a specific aesthetic, lifestyle, or vibe.

_Her outfits are very cottagecore lately._

**Crash out** – To get mad or upset despite your better judgment.

_This game is making me so mad, I’m about to **crash out**._

**Cray cray –** Short for crazy.

_I’ve been so busy this week, it’s_ **_cray cray_** _!_

**Cringe –** A feeling of embarrassment and discomfort.

_Watching Annie try to talk to James was so **cringe.**_

**Twin –** A true friend or friend that is so close that the two share a long list of interests, experiences, or characteristics.

_Hey_ **_twin_** _, when you comin’ over?_

**Twizzy –** Variation of twin (see above).

_Hey_ **_twizzy_** _, when you comin’ over?_

* * *

## _U-Z_

* * *

### U

* * *

**Uhh** – Used to express confusion, sometimes in response to a joke that doesn’t make sense.

Person 1: _Don’t you think my post was so funny? Didn’t you get it?_

Person 2: _**Uhh** . . ._

**Unalive –** A substitute for “kill,” “die,” or “suicide,” created to get around social media filters that flag those words. Because it’s designed to avoid detection, parents should take any references seriously and check in with their child.

_If your teen uses_ **_unalive_** _when talking about themselves, it’s worth a gentle, direct conversation._

**Unc –** Short for uncle, used to refer to a cool millennial uncle or to refer to slightly older people in general.

_Just walking up those stairs made me so tired, I think I’ve reached_ **_unc_** _status._

**Understood the assignment –** When someone goes above and beyond.

_This was the best birthday ever! You definitely_ **_understood the assignment_** _._

**Upper decky** – A term for a Zyn (nicotine pouch) that’s placed against the upper gums.

_I don’t think I’ve ever seen Heidi without an **upper decky.**_

* * *

### V

**V –** Abbreviation for Very.

_I’m_ **_v_** _excited for prom next weekend._

**Vanilla –** Ordinary, boring, lacking special features.

_I tried having a conversation with him, but he’s so_ **_vanilla_** _._

**Vibe –** A feeling, an ambience.

_I love your whole_ **_vibe_** _._

**VSCO girl –**(pronounced visco), A young, usually white, girl who is adorned in trendy things and posts pictures edited on the VSCO app.

_She’s wearing an oversized t-shirt, Birks, and has a huge Hydro Flask. She’s definitely trying to be a_ **_VSCO girl_** _._

* * *

### W

**W –** Win, Winner.

_Our team took the_ **_W_** _._

**Wallflower –** An introvert, someone who avoids the limelight and is more comfortable standing on the sidelines of an activity.

_She’s always been a_ **_wallflower_** _at school dances._

**Weird flex but ok –** Used to acknowledge someone’s unusual statement or action, typically in response to the boasting or showing off. A light-hearted way to express acceptance or indifference to something that might be considered odd.

_You can brag about your collection of rubber ducks all you want._ **_Weird flex, but ok_** _._

**Whip –** A car, especially one that is stylish.

_She just pulled up in her new_ **_whip_** _._

**Whole meal** – Describes someone who looks really good.

_Dave looks like a **whole meal**._

**Wig snatched –** Extreme excitement or astonishment, especially in response to something surprising, impressive, or unexpected. Comes from the idea that something is so amazing that it figuratively causes one’s wig to fly off in amazement.

_When he hit that high note during the performance, my_ **_wig was snatched_** _._

**Woke –** Someone who is aware of important facts, and racial and social injustices.

_I used to be ignorant of what was happening around me, but now I’m_ **_woke_** _._

**WYA –** An acronym that stands for Where you at? Commonly used in text messages to ask someone about their current location.

_Let me know_ **_wya_** _and I’ll come meet up._

**WYD –** An acronym that stands for What you doing? A casual way to ask someone what they are currently doing.

**_WYD_** _tonight?_

* * *

### X

**Xan –** Abbreviation for: Xanax, a sedative used to treat anxiety which is often abused.

_I hope his dad finally realizes who’s been stealing his_ **_xan_** _._

* * *

### Y

**YAAS –** An enthusiastic way of saying “yes.” Used to express excitement, approval, or agreement.

**_Yaas_** _, queen! Way to nail that dance routine._

**Yeet** – To throw something forcefully.

_He just **yeeted** a peanut butter jar out the window._

* * *

### Z

**Zaddy** – A handsome, fashionable, older man.

_She found a **zaddy** as soon as she graduated._

**Zombie –** Someone who “ghosted” you (disappeared with no explanation) and then suddenly reappears in your messages as if nothing happened.

_He ghosted me in March and just texted “hey” — total_ **_zombie_** _._

* * *

### Numerical Slang

**41 –** A viral number with no fixed meaning, used as a nonsense comeback or joke. It spread through a rap song and is often paired with “6-7.”

_“What’s the answer to number three?” “_ **_41_** _!”_

**6-7** – Doesn’t have a specific meaning. A viral way teens are responding to any question. Said in a sing-songy way, while doing a gesture with both hands as if weighing two options.

“ _How are you doing?_“

“6-7”

* * *

### Parents Can Better Support Kids Through Slang

All kids want love and [attention from their parents](https://gabb.com/blog/4-parenting-styles/) in real life, even if they don’t always seem like they do. When we take the time to learn about the way our children speak, it shows kids that we prioritize our relationship and [communication](https://gabb.com/).

[![getting lost in all this slang keep your kid safe and yourself sane with gabb messenger](https://gabb.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/11/25-Teen-Slang-inset-image-1200x400-v2-1024x341.png)](https://gabb.com/gabb-messenger/?utm_source=Blog&utm_medium=Blog&utm_campaign=TEENSLANG)

We can use appropriate slang words once in a while to make our kids laugh. Use it correctly, or not — kids will appreciate the effort. NGL, our teens may roll their eyes and call us thirsty, but we all know deep down they think we’re fire.

If you are looking for more information about [texting acronyms and abbreviations](https://gabb.com/blog/text-slang/) feel free to read our other article.

What is your experience with teen slang? Share your stories in the comments

## Frequently Asked Questions

**What is Gen Z slang?**

Gen Z slang is the ever-changing set of words, phrases, and acronyms used by people born roughly between 1997 and 2012. Much of it starts on platforms like TikTok, YouTube, and Instagram, then spreads fast. Some terms are shortened words or acronyms, while others are ordinary words given brand-new meanings.

**What are the most popular teen slang words right now?**

Some of the most common terms in 2026 include 6-7, aura, delulu, glazing, and standing on business. Because slang moves quickly, we update this guide regularly — the full A–Z list above covers 200+ current terms with definitions and examples.

**Which teen slang words should parents pay attention to?**

A handful can signal situations worth a gentle check-in: “KMS,” “KYS,” and “unalive” reference self-harm or suicide (often as a joke, but not always); “sneaky link” means a secret hookup; “plug” can refer to a drug source; and “trap phone” means a hidden second phone. Spotting these isn’t cause for panic — they’re just good conversation starters.

**How is Gen Z slang different from millennial slang?**

Millennial slang leaned on full phrases and early-internet acronyms like “LOL” and “on fleek.” Gen Z slang moves faster, is more meme- and video-driven, and often repurposes everyday words like “mid,” “cooked,” and “aura.” Some terms carry over, which is why you’ll see overlap.

**Where do teens learn new slang?**

Mostly from social media — TikTok, YouTube, Instagram, Twitch, and group chats — plus music and online gaming. A word can go from one viral video to everyday use in a matter of weeks.

**How often is this list updated?**

Regularly. We add new terms as they emerge and trends shift, so it’s worth checking back. It currently includes 200+ terms.

Keeping up with internet slang can sometimes feel like learning a whole new language, especially with the rate at which new slang words come and go. In 2025 alone, the Oxford English Dictionary added over 500 words and phrases\[1\], crowning ‘rage bait’ their word of the year\[2\] – much to many people’s surprise.

One minute we’re coming to terms with ‘6-7’ and ‘rage bait’, and the next we’re being told that ‘the saxophones are getting louder’, wondering what it is that’s actually happening.

So, we’ve rounded up some of the most viral words and phrases we’ve heard this year, creating a cheat sheet to 2026 slang, because nobody wants to be ‘cringe’.

## **Preply’s 2026 slang dictionary**

![Preply’s 2026 slang dictionary](https://preply.com/wp-content/uploads/Preplys-2026-slang-dictionary.png)

From TikTok viral ‘boy kibble’ to the World Cup’s ‘Mbappé special’, we analysed the new and quirky slang terms that have somehow made their way into our everyday conversations, as Madeline Enos, language trends expert here at Preply, shares expert insights into the phrases.

![](https://preply.com/wp-content/themes/peply-blog-v4.0/assets/img/del/campaign__Kariamny.png)

Online lessons

Learn a language with personalised 1-on-1 classes with our expert tutors from all over the world

[English tutors online](https://preply.com/en/online/english-tutors) [French tutors online](https://preply.com/en/online/french-tutors) [Spanish tutors online](https://preply.com/en/online/spanish-tutors)

## **Emerging slang trends for 2026**

1. **Biggest year-on-year spike:** ‘The saxophones are getting louder’ surged 12,959% in search interest in 2026 – no other slang word or phrase tracked came close.
2. **Highest search volume overall:** ‘LARP’ pulled in 1.1 million worldwide searches in 2026, making it the most-searched slang term on this list by raw volume.

### **January**

#### **1\. Lowkenuinely**

**_Worldwide searches for ‘lowkenuinely’ peaked in January 2026, reaching 22,000 searches._**

**Preply’s definition:** ‘Lowkenuinely’ means to tell the truth or share information in a sincere, calm, or laid-back way.

**Where did ‘lowkenuinely’ come from?** _“‘Lowkenuinely’ is a combination of the slang phrase ‘lowkey’, meaning to be quiet or subtle, and ‘genuinely’, meaning sincerely. The phrase originates from TikTok, where Gen Z may say ‘I lowkenuinely love this song’, being a softer alternative to ‘actually’ or ‘seriously’, which are typically used to express a strong opinion.”_

### **February**

#### **2\. Cortisol spike**

**_**_Worldwide searches for ‘cortisol spike’ were up by 161% in three months, hitting 81,000 searches in February 2026._**_**

**Preply’s definition:**‘Cortisol spike’ is a viral internet joke used to describe moments of shock, embarrassment, or awkwardness.

**Where did ‘cortisol spike’ come from?** _“The phrase ‘cortisol spike’ originated as a joke on X in early 2025, used humorously to refer to stressful or embarrassing situations. In early 2026, the phrase became a widespread viral internet expression, often paired with a fake or exaggerated ‘cortisol meter’ meme. Now, the slang phrase has evolved further into two variations: ‘high cortisol’, referring to high anxiety and stress, while ‘low cortisol’ refers to calm or nonchalant behaviour.”_

### **March**

#### **3\. Boy kibble**

**_Worldwide searches for ‘boykibble’ spiked by 123% in March, hitting 29,000 searches._**

**Preply’s definition:** ‘Boy kibble’ is a viral social media food featuring simple, high-protein meals, typically including ground meat and white rice.

**Where did ‘boy kibble’ come from?** _“Boy kibble is a new playful take on ‘girl dinner’. Where ‘girl dinner’ typically consists of random snacks or bits and pieces from the fridge, ‘boy dinner’ is the opposite, made up of plain, highly-functioning ingredients. The contrast between ‘girl dinner’ and the new ‘boy kibble’ demonstrates Gen Z’s natural embrace of protein, in a tongue-in-cheek, humorous way by comparing ground beef and white rice to dog food.”_

#### **4\. Future Faking**

**_UK searches for ‘future faking’ up by 94% on the previous year in March 2026._**

**Preply’s definition:** ‘Future faking’ refers to a behaviour where someone provides empty promises for the future to get something they presently want.

**Where did ‘future faking’ come from?** _“‘Future faking’ is a modern term which acts to summarise a large set of behaviours displayed early in a relationship. This may reflect a broader cultural shift within modern dating towards passive, non-committal language.”_

#### **5\. The saxophones are getting louder**

**_Worldwide searches for ‘the saxophones are getting louder’ were up by 12,959% over the previous year in 2026._**

**Preply’s definition:** ‘The saxophones are getting louder’ means that something bad, negative, or inevitable is getting closer.

**Where did ‘the saxophones are getting louder’ come from?** _“The ‘saxophones getting louder’ grew from the famous 1991 film, Boyz n the Hood, where swelling saxophones foreshadow a dramatic shooting. Now, with TikTok users making videos to the sound, it’s become a viral meme used to signal impending doom, from falling down the stairs to accidentally spending too much money in a restaurant.”_

### **April**

#### **6\. Looksmaxxing**

**_**_Worldwide searches for ‘looksmaxxing’ were up by 149% since January 2026, hitting 399,000 searches in April 2026._**_**

**Preply’s definition:**‘Looksmaxxing’ refers to trying to improve someone’s physical appearance or attractiveness as much as possible.

**Where did  ‘looksmaxxing’  come from?** _“‘Looksmaxxing’ emerged from TikTok and social media online subcultures focused on maximising physical appearance through facial features, height, jawlines, and skin. This slang suffix (often used as -maxxing) has rapidly evolved into a much wider cultural phenomenon, driven by social media algorithms and digital-first communication.”_

#### **7\. 7×7=49**

**_Worldwide searches for ‘7×7 49’ were up by 565% on the previous year, hitting 21,000 searches in April 2026._**

**Preply’s definition:** ‘7x’7=49’ is a viral TikTok meme and shorthand slang used to describe something or someone that is extremely attractive.

**Where did ‘7×7=49’ come from?** _“The equation ‘7×7=49’ became TikTok viral after users jokingly shared that they found the equation attractive, transforming an ordinary maths equation into a hilarious internet meme. While it may seem absurd, this phrase is Gen Z’s new way of saying ‘hear me out’, giving everyday words, or even numbers, a new meaning through humour and shared understanding.”_

#### **8\. Everything Hallelujah**

**_Worldwide searches for ‘everything hallelujah’ were up by 1,519% on the previous year, hitting 191,000 searches in April 2026._**

**Preply’s definition:** ‘Everything hallelujah’ is typically used after a short sentence or statement to celebrate everyday micro-wins and express gratitude.

**Where did ‘everything hallelujah’ come from?** _“Following Justin Bieber’s viral Coachella performance of ‘Everything Hallelujah’, fans began using the phrase as a casual suffix, adding ‘hallelujah’ to the end of simple sentences. Even Hailey Bieber jumped in on the trend, posting on TikTok ‘Rhodes eye patches hallelujah’ and ‘sweet treat hallelujah’, as fans embrace the phrase as a simple way to express gratitude.”_

### **May**

#### **9\. Mogging**

**_**_Worldwide searches for ‘mogging’ were up by 203% since January 2026, hitting 566,000 searches in May 2026._**_**

**Preply’s definition:** ‘‘Mogging’ is a viral TikTok phrase meaning to outshine or look significantly better than someone else.

**Where did ‘mogging’ come from?** _“The slang phrase ‘mogging’ has an interesting history, growing from the acronym ‘AMOG’, meaning ‘Alpha Male Of the Group’, which originated from pick-up artist communities and bodybuilding forums. In recent years, the term has spread across social media platforms, particularly TikTok, as Gen Z picked up the slang phrase ‘mogging’ and made it their own. The phrase now refers to outperforming others in physical appearance, often used jokingly online.”_

#### **10\. You the birthday**

**_Worldwide searches for ‘you the birthday’ peaked in May 2026, hitting 910,000 searches._**

**Preply’s definition:** ‘You the birthday’ is a compliment to say that someone is the ‘main character’ or main attention of the room.

**Where did ‘you the birthday’ come from?** _“‘You the birthday’ is a classic example of Gen Z’s vague and quirky communication style. Essentially, it’s another ‘6-7’ case, where the phrase itself is commonly used without real meaning acting as a compliment.”_

### **June**

#### **11\. LARP**

**_Worldwide Google searches for ‘LARP’ were up by 195% over the previous year, hitting 1,100,000 searches in April 2026._**

**Preply’s definition:** ‘LARP’ is used as an adjective to describe someone who is perceived to be performative.

**Where did ‘LARP’ come from?** _“The phrase ‘LARP’ is originally derived from the acronym meaning Live Action Role Play, a hobby where individuals dress up and act out fictional scenarios. Now, ‘LARP’ has evolved and become a prominent fixture in internet slang, showing how quickly a niche acronym can enter everyday urban lingo. The transition from an acronym to an adjective clearly demonstrates social media’s significant impact on real-world language trends, where online subcultures drive language change.”_

### **July**

#### **12\. Mbappé special**

**_Worldwide Google searches for ‘Mbappé special’ skyrocketed by 233% in July, reaching 14,000 searches._**

**Preply’s definition:** The ‘Mbappé special’ simply translates to ‘nothing’, used playfully by users on social media when someone or something has quite literally done nothing.

**Where did ‘Mbappé special’ come from?** _“The ‘Mbappé special’ originates from a viral interview with Vanity Fair, where, after revealing he is learning to cook, Kylian Mbappé is asked what the ‘Mbappé special’ is. The football star went viral after responding ‘for example, nothing’, gaining 19.4 million views. This viral meme stretched beyond social media, with football fans using the ‘Mbappé special’ to express disappointment in players’ performances at the World Cup.”_

#### **13\. Quiet on the creek**

**_Worldwide searches for ‘quiet on the creek’ spiked by 8,300% in July 2026, reaching 512,000 searches._**

**Preply’s definition:** The phrase ‘quiet on the creek’ means to be quiet or keep something to yourself.

**Where did ‘quiet on the creek’ come from?** _“The TikTok-born slang originates from a viral video by American rapper Saucy Santana, who on a TikTok live, while eating food, explained ‘I used to go fishing when I was a little girl, you gotta be real quiet on the creek’._

_“The expression directly draws from the idea that if somebody is too loud while fishing, they’ll scare the fish away. As internet slang, users came to interpret the phrase as meaning to keep their plans, achievements, or relationships private, rather than public.”_

### **August**

#### **14\. Polyester**

_**Worldwide searches for ‘polyester slang’ spiked by 141% in a single week in August 2026, up by 1,292% over the previous year.**_

**Preply’s definition:** ‘Polyester’ is used as a critique to call out content that is perceived as low-quality, generic, or inauthentic online.

**Where did ‘polyester’ come from?** _“‘Polyester’ is the internet’s latest slang term, giving a familiar word a new meaning. Traditionally, polyester is a synthetic material commonly used in affordable (and often mass-produced) clothing, but now it’s taking on a whole new meaning. The term has gained traction among Gen Z, calling out polyester lifestyles, videos, and even people, reflecting a wider Gen Z preference for authenticity over polished perfection online.”_

#### **15\. Meat Proxy**

**_Worldwide searches for ‘meat proxy’ were up by 1,847% over the previous year, hitting 14,000 searches in August 2026._**

**Preply’s definition:** ‘Meat proxy’ refers to someone who forwards or uses AI-generated content without reading, understanding, or editing it.

**Where did ‘meat proxy’ come from?** _“‘Meat proxy’ is a quickly emerging corporate and tech slang phrase for AI users. Widely thought to be coined by developer Niklas Guhn, the phrase reflects a wider attitude towards artificial intelligence in professional environments, where ‘meat proxy’ becomes a way to express frustration with the disappearance of authenticity in light of more AI content.”_

### **September**

#### **16\. That’s so AI**

_**_Worldwide searches for ‘that’s so AI’ were up by 178% over the previous year, hitting 21,000 searches in September 2026._**_

**Preply’s definition:**‘That’s so AI’ is a popular Gen Alpha insult referring to something that is fake or low-quality.

**Where did ‘that’s so AI’ come from?** _“The slang phrase ‘that’s so AI’ grew from Gen Alpha’s perception of artificial intelligence as low-quality and fake-looking. Now, ‘that’s so AI’ doesn’t necessarily mean that something was actually created with AI. More young people are increasingly using the phrase as an insult to call out fake, unbelievable, or phoney behaviour more broadly.”_

## What 2026 slang tells us about language

Slang might come and go, but it shows us something bigger: language never stands still. From TikTok trends to football interviews, the words we use evolve with our culture, communities, and conversations. Keeping up isn’t about knowing every viral phrase. It’s about understanding how people really communicate. And whether you’re learning a new language or simply trying to make sense of your feed, every new expression is another way to connect.

If you’re trying to decode what your teen means by “rizz”, “brain rot” or “sigma”, you’re not alone.

At luna, we hear from thousands of UK teens every day through our app and teen ambassador community.

They’ve told us the slang they actually use in 2026, what it means, and how it shows up in real conversations.

This guide is designed for parents: an on-the-pulse, teen-approved dictionary you can dip into whenever a new phrase appears in your house, on TikTok, or in your teen’s group chat.

If you want more, you can also discover the [**emojis teens are using right now**](https://weareluna.app/parents/guides/navigating-difficult-scenarios/teen-emoji-dictionary/)via our guide, or the [**text acronyms**](https://weareluna.app/parents/guides/navigating-difficult-scenarios/text-acronyms-guide/) they use in messages, captions and DMs.

**What is teen slang?**

Teen slang is the constantly changing set of words, phrases and in-jokes teens use to express feelings, rate people and react to what they see online.

**Examples of highly popular 2026 teen slang include:**

- **“Rizz”:** short for charisma; having game or charm
- **“Ate” / “She ate”:** did something really well
- **“Brain rot”:** watching or quoting too much mindless content
- **“Skibidi”:** nonsense word used as a meme or random reaction
- **“Sigma”:** independent, confident, “main character” energy
- **"6 7":** used as a nonsense punchline or shouted out when the number appears e.g. on a maths board at school

![](https://www.datocms-assets.com/108981/1784910241-teen-girl-slang-phone-call.png?auto=format)

**How to use this teen slang guide**

Not all slang is a red flag. A lot of it is silly, creative and harmless. Some terms, though, can hint at:

- **Online bullying or exclusion** (e.g. how slang is used in comment sections or group chats)
- **Body image or food worries**
- **Low mood or “brain rot”-style burnout**

Where it’s relevant, we’ve added a short note under the definition to flag when a phrase might be linked to bullying, mental health, or online pressure – plus other parent guides you can read if you’re concerned.

**Numbers**

[**“67” / “6-7”**](https://weareluna.app/parents/guides/teen-news-and-insights/parents-guide-to-6-7-trend/): a viral TikTok meme that comes from the drill song _Doot Doot_ by Skrilla, where the lyrics repeat “six” and “seven”; it doesn’t actually mean anything, but teens use it as a nonsense punchline or random response to questions (similar to the _skibidi_ meme); on TikTok it’s often said with a specific exaggerated voice and paired with a hand gesture (palms up, moving up and down);“What time is it?” “67.”

**Slang words beginning with A**

**“Aight”:** equivalent to “okay”; “That’s aight”

**“Alpha”:** often referring to a crush, someone who’s powerful or dominant in social settings; often used by Generation Alpha (0-15 years old); “He is such an Alpha”

**“As \[expletive\]” (AF):** used to agree with someone or something or to emphasise; “that’s cool af”

**"Ate":** means someone did something really well; “She ate down with that outfit”

**"Aura" or "Aura points":** if you do something embarrassing or humbling you essentially lose aura points, and if you do something good or cool you gain aura points – a good example is on social media you’ll find lots of videos where people write “how many aura points did I lose when I did \[insert humbling story\]”

**Slang words beginning with B**

**“Bae”:** cute nickname to describe a significant other; used along baby or babe; “They're my bae”

**“Banger”:** used to describe an amazing song; “Mamma Mia by ABBA is such a banger”

**“Based”:** when you agree with the argument, when the argument is grounded in factual statements; “Dude your take on dogs is based”

**“Basic”:** something unextraordinary, boring, lacklustre, often used to describe a person or a cultural thing; “She is so basic, I saw her with her pumpkin spiced latte yesterday”, "I can't believe people like \[insert artist name\], they're so basic"

**“Beef”:** having drama with someone, having a feud; “I don’t want to go to the party with her, she and I have beef”

**"Be for real" (BFR):** a call for honesty or to stop exaggerating, often calling another out; used more commonly in BFFR (Be \[expletive\] For Real); “Bestie BFR, that outfit wasn't as bad as you're saying it was”

**“Bed rotting” sometimes “Rotting":** popularised on social media, this means staying in bed all day, often on devices, and not practising self care or avoiding responsibilities – sometimes due to a poor mood, or just not feeling up to doing anything; bed rotting can be used lightly as a term, but also more seriously and in this case it isn't often about being lazy or avoiding basic hygiene, and instead it can be a sign of more serious mental health struggles in which the priority is to get through the day, and all other forms of self-care are set to the side. If you’re worried this might apply to your teen, our guide on [**bed rotting and teen mental health**](https://weareluna.app/parents/guides/mental-health-and-wellbeing/bed-rotting-meaning/)explains what it can mean and when to seek help; “I'm stuck in a cycle of bed rotting”

**“Beige flag”:** quirky behaviour or attributes, often in a romantic partner, that are neither positive (green) nor negative (red), little quirks that make you go "Hug...that's something!"; “He claps when the plane lands – to me that's such a beige flag”

**“Beg” or “Beggy”:** used to describe someone who is too eager to gain attention, approval, or material benefits from others, often seen as insincere or desperate; “He's being so beggy”

**“Bet”:** to go for it or used to say “ok”; “Hey, we're going to the movies, wanna come?” “Bet”

**“Big yikes”:** something extremely embarrassing; “I literally crashed and spilled my drink all over my crush yesterday” “Big yikes”

**“Bounce”:** to go somewhere, to head somewhere else; “Gotta bounce”

**“Brain rot”:** Oxford Dictionary definition = “the supposed deterioration of a person’s mental or intellectual state, especially viewed as the result of overconsumption of material (now particularly online content) considered to be trivial or unchallenging"; “You literally speak in brain rot;” if you’re hearing this a lot at home and are unsure how worried to be, our guide to [**brain rot and whether it’s real**](https://weareluna.app/parents/guides/mental-health-and-wellbeing/teen-brain-rot/)breaks down what teens mean by it and how screen time can affect them

**“Brat” or "Brat summer":** no longer just a term used to describe a petulant person, this has expanded to a new meaning, credited to performer Charlie XCX through the marketing of her album "Brat"; it means going against the grain, doing the unexpected, messiness, creativity, and self-expression – a resistance to all things curated, "perfect" and conventional; “She literally looks so brat with her hair like that”

**“Brokie”:** someone who does not have sufficient funds; “I spent all my money on Taylor Swift tickets, now I’m a brokie”

**“Bruh”:** equivalent to dude; “Bruh, leave me alone!”

**“Bussin’”:** something delicious, usually said in the context of food; “This sushi is bussin’.”

**Slang words beginning with C**

**“Canon event”:** a moment that built character in someone’s life; “It’s fine, getting a detention from Mrs. Evans is a canon event all year 9s have to go through”

**“Cap”:** used to call someone out for their lie, something that is not true; “Dude that’s cap, you did not say that to him”

**“Caught in 4k”:** getting exposed; “I caught you in 4k flirting with that guy”

![](https://www.datocms-assets.com/108981/1784910327-teen-slang-phone-chart.png?auto=format)

**“Cheugy”:** something old and not cool; “Owl pendant necklaces are so cheugy”

**“Chuzz”:** a derogatory slang term that comes from _“chopped huzz”_, meaning an unattractive girl; “huzz” itself is a disrespectful term for women, and “chuzz” is used to insult someone’s appearance, often in comment sections or as a put-down in videos; “Someone just commented ‘chuzz’ on my post”

**“Clapped”:** has multiple meanings, but in the UK it mostly means insulting someone for their looks; “Damn you used your bike so much, its clapped”

**“Clown”:** used to describe someone who is a fool or to describe oneself in internet culture when they've been taken for a fool e.g. in a romantic context; “He made me feel like such a clown”

**"Cooked":** this can mean "you’re done" or "that’s over"; loss of hope over a situation; “I’m so cooked for this test tomorrow, I didn’t study”

**“Cope”:** used to finish an argument, can be interchangeable with “agree to disagree” or "deal with it"; “I’m done arguing, cope”

**“Cringe”:** something embarrassing, gives a feeling of repulsion; “That’s so cringe, please stop”

**“Cursed”:** describing something off-putting, creepy almost; “Dude, your avatar looks cursed”

**“Curve”:** to ignore/reject somebody's romantic advances; “I curved him after he said he wanted to go to the movies, I don’t want a relationship”

**Slang words beginning with D**

**“Dank”:** something cool and original/niche; “I only make dank memes”

**“Dead”:** laughing so much to the point of almost “dying”; “I’M DEAD!”

**“Deadass”:** to be so serious; “Dude, deadass, I passed all my A-levels even without studying hard”

**“Deets”:** short for details; “Please give me all the deets about the date”

**“Delulu”:** short for delusion, ignorance is bliss; “I know he isn’t into me, but I will remain delulu”

**“Demure”:** popularised recently on social media, this means being mindful, considerate and modest – often used to explain how someone has dealt with a tricky situation e.g. a disagreement at school or a public breakup; “See how I handled that breakup? Very demure, very maturely, very quietly”

**“Diff”:** short for difference; “What’s the diff between cap and BFR?”

**“Do it for the Plot”:** encouraging crazy behaviour for the story it could lead to, such as sending risky texts to friends or crushes; “Girl, do it for the plot and ask him out”

**“Dope”:** something cool; “That new bag is so dope”

**“Down bad”:** being silently desperate to be in a relationship; “I’m so down bad for him, I think I will do anything for him to ask me out”

**“Drip”:** to describe someone’s outfit as cool; “He has some insane drip”

**“Dub”:** another term for win, interchangeable with “W”; “We won 10-6, we took the dub!”

**“Dusty”:** used as an insult and describes someone as unkept/unclean; “I won’t go with him, he is so dusty”

**Slang words beginning with E**

**“Eepy”:** short for sleepy; “My dog is so eepy”

**“Extra”:** used to describe a person who is trying too hard or going too far; “My brother's so extra, just do the chores mum asked you to do, no need to kick up a fuss”

**Slang words beginning with F**

**“Feral”:** used in past tense when someone acted crazy; “I will go feral if we don’t leave school early”

**“Flex”:** to brag; “Not to flex on you guys, but my mum got me that trending teen skincare product”

**“Flick”:** short for picture; “Did you get flicks of that outfit you wore last night?”

“ **Flop era”:** being stuck in a rut; “It's time I set some new goals and leave my flop era”

**“Finesse”:** scheming your way out of a system, being slick; “Ima finesse my way around to get some free movie tickets”

**“Fire”:** used to flatter or describe something in a positive way; “Dude that’s so fire”

**“Fit”:** UK slang for someone who is good looking; or short for outfit; “Love the 'fit”, “I fancy them, they're fit”

**“Fit check”:** showing off your outfit, or multiple outfits, often in a social media video; “Fit check!”

**"FR":** short for "for real," used to agree with someone; “OMG, I FR feel the same way about them”

**“Function”:** used in the context of “pulling up to the function”, a party

**Slang words beginning with G**

**“Gas”:** being satisfied or describing something insanely good, used in the context of food; “This food is gas, ima order another set of dumplings”

**“Ghosted”:** to be left on read by a crush, cutting ties off abruptly; “I got ghosted by Jake, I’m so sad :(“

**“Giving”/ “It’s giving”:**“it’s giving” means something is generally positive; also used to describe other connotations, so “it’s giving alpha” might mean something is giving powerful vibes; “It’s giving brat”

**“Glazed”:** overpraising or hyping something/someone excessively, often when it’s not actually that impressive; can imply bias or trying too hard; “Why are you glazing that person so much?”, “The teacher was glazing her in class”

**“Glow up”:** when someone changes their look, a positive transformation mentally and physically; “She had such a glow up during the summer, I wonder if its because of football camp”

**“GOATEST”:** an exaggerated version of G.O.A.T. (Greatest of All Time), meaning someone or something that is the absolute best; “David Beckham is the GOATEST”

**“Goblin mode”:** going “crazy” or “insane”, losing it; meant to describe someone’s state of mind/persona; “I’m about to go full on Goblin Mode for this party tonight”, "My cat got the zoomies and went full Goblin Mode"

**“Go off”:** about to go on a tirade/rant; “I will go off on Josie if she flakes on my birthday party tonight”

**“Grind”:** to work hard; “I’m grinding to finish this essay for tonight”

**“Gucci”:** used to describe state of being in a positive light; “it’s all good”=”it’s all gucci”

**“Gyatt”:** used to express excitement, surprise, or admiration, often as an exclamation in reaction to seeing a large bum or curvy figure – it's often used as a noun and a hashtag; “GYATT! She is fine”

**Slang words beginning with H**

**“Hits different” / "Hits diff":** usually used positively, when something feels different in different contexts; “Cold water hits different after a nap”

**“Hop off”:** wanting someone to log offline; “Hop off the chat pls, you’re being annoying”

**“Hype”:** to describe something excitingly or something popular; “I finally get the hype of the Borough Market strawberries”, "I finally get the Stanley Cup hype"

**"Huzz":** a slang term teens are using to refer to girls, comes from an internet-mangled version of hoes – which is a disrespectful American slang word for women; you can read more in our guide on [**what your teen means by “huzz”**](https://weareluna.app/parents/guides/navigating-difficult-scenarios/huzz-meaning/)

**Slang words beginning with I**

**“Ick”:** an action that your crush does that “turns you off”, often quite petty in context and generally comedic in nature; “The way she tripped gave me the ick”, "I got the ick when I say him read the chocolate box card before choosing his chocolate"

**“IRL” (In Real Life):** used to differentiate between situations or friendships that are online or in real life; “My IRL friends literally do not know I secretly play League of Legends”

**"Iykyk" (if you know, you know):** used for inside jokes or shared knowledge of context; “ “Only real ones know about Josie’s birthday, ifykyk”

**Slang words beginning with J**

**"Jarring":** annoying or agitating; “Man don't be so jarring…”

**Slang words beginning with K**

**“Karen”:** used in the context of someone who complains or is simply rude; was originally used offensively to describe a middle aged woman who is rude and entitled (main catchphrase is “I want the manager”); “Ugh, my mom is being such a Karen, I just wanted to go out”

**“Kinda ate”:** negative connotation to ate, or when someone surprisingly ate when they didn't intend to/weren't expected to; “I know that outfit was weird but you kinda ate"

**Slang words beginning with L**

**"Leave":** used to indicate someone is being annoying or embarrassing; “Leave – you’re being so annoying”

**“Lit”:** the short form of literally or something that is “fire”, something that is cool; “Dude that jacket is lit”, "Lit cannot explain how stressed I am rn"

**“L/ Take the L”:** means losing/loser, accepting a loss; “Take the L my guy, there's no coming back from that”

**“LMAO” (Laughing My Ass Off):** used interchangeably with dead, laughing but in an ironic sense; “LMAO, there's no way you spilled your drink on him”

**“Locked in”:** in a groove, getting the hang of something, being super concentrated; “I have to lock in for this exam, if not I fail the entire course”

**“Lore”:** background information on someone or something often going back years; possibly secrets or in the case of celebrities, things that the true fans would know; “Spencer Pratt lore is the craziest lore”

**“LOML” (love of my life):** a soulmate, used platonically or romantically, mostly used platonically; “Ashley is literally the LOML, we’ve been besties since primary school”, more recently the meaning could also indicate "loss of my life" since Taylor Swift released the song "loml"

**Lowkenuinely:** a mash-up of **“lowkey”** and **“genuinely”**, used to emphasise that someone _actually_ means what they’re saying, often in a slightly ironic or self-aware way; “Lowkeinly, that was the best pizza I’ve ever had”

**“Lowkey”:** to play down the intensity of someone’s emotions or opinions or to keep things on the down low/secret; usually said in this manner “Lowkey I want some ice cream", "Lowkey I do not like them”

**Slang words beginning with M**

**"Mango mustard":** a Gen-Alpha “brain-rot” meme built on a stupid-on-purpose word joke – _mango_ has six letters and _mustard_ has seven, which together become “67;” the phrase pops up in hyperactive, glitch-heavy edits, chaotic memes (often referencing Kendrick Lamar yelling “Mustard”), and phonk remix videos (it’s intentionally nonsensical – equal parts ironic cringe and absurd humour)

**"Mental":** used as slang for something crazy or unexpected; “That’s mental that she made so much money selling sweets online”

**“Mid”:** means mediocre; “That show is mid”

**“Mogging”:** showing off your looks to seem superior; “Dude stop mogging, no one is impressed”

**“Moment”:** usually referring to a drama or something being spotlit, can be used to set something in context; "You're having a moment", "I'm having a Mariah Carey moment"

**“Mood”:** usually used as a response after relating to something someone else has said; “No bc that is literally a mood”

**“Mute”:** used to ignore someone online; “I’m muting this convo”

**Slang words beginning with N**

**"NBSB" (No Boyfriend Since Birth):** used to describe someone who has never had a boyfriend; can be said jokingly, self-deprecatingly, or simply as a matter-of-fact statement about relationship experience; “I’m NBSB, so I don’t really know what to expect”

**“Neek”**: UK slang (a blend of “nerd” and “geek”) used to describe someone who's overly studious, socially awkward, or seen as trying too hard to follow rules or be “perfect”; can be used jokingly between friends or as a mild insult; “Stop revising on a Friday night, you’re such a neek”

**“NGL” (not gonna lie):** used as “just saying” or “no offence”, giving your opinion; “NGL, I don’t like her vibe”

**“No cap”:** not lying; “That food was so good, no cap”

**“Noob”:** a novice, often used in a gaming context for newbies; “You’re such a noob at this game”

**“No thoughts, head empty”:** used to describe someone dumb, said after saying something dumb or describing a state of mind; “Dude don’t talk I’m no thoughts, head empty”

**“Normie”:** describing someone who is out of touch within online culture, someone who tends to follow the status quo; “You’re such a normie you only like chart music”

**“NPC”:** in a context of a game it means “non-playable character”, teenagers apply this to someone who has no personality/bland; “They're such an NPC, that group just stands there and doesn’t move”

**Slang words beginning with O**

**“Ohio”:** not just a US state, but a synonym for anything strange or a bit cringey – used as an adjective; “That’s Ohio”

**“OP”**: short for _overpowered_; used to describe someone or something that’s unfairly good, dominant, or doing “too much” in a funny or impressed way – originally from gaming (where an OP weapon or character is too strong), Gen Alpha uses it more broadly to hype people, skills, outfits, or moments; “that comeback was OP”, “her confidence is OP”, “this filter is OP”

**“OOMF”:** used to mean One Of My Friends; “When OOMF tells me they have a crush on someone”

**“OMG” (oh my god/gosh):** said in state of shock or surprise; “OMG, I have to tell you something!”

**“ONG” (on god):** used to swear by; “ONG I am not lying”

**“On point”:** close to perfection; “That is so on point”

**“Outta pocket”:** someone or a phrase that is said out of context; or something said controversially; “That comment was so outta pocket”

**Slang words beginning with P**

**“Periodt”:** meaning period, said at the end of a statement; “Periodt, queen! You left them speechless”

**“Pink tote lid moment”:** a social media trend in which teens, as well as adults on a smaller scale, share unsettling stories about their experiences arguing and disagreeing with a parent; “That is such a Pink Tote Lid Moment”

**“Pookie”:** another term of endearment for either a partner or friend; “They are my pookies, I don’t go anywhere without my besties”

**“POV” (“Point Of View):** usually said in memes or videos filmed from the angle of the creator; “POV: you’re waking up in the morning”

**“Preppy”:** more recently a type of fashion trend with pastels, gingham and basic styles; “I do not like the Preppy fashion”

**“Pushing P”:** used when something is going great, can be used interchangeably with fire; “Literally pushing P”

**Slang words beginning with Q**

**Queer:** an umbrella term that many LGBTQ+ people use to describe their sexual orientation or gender identity – today, lots of young people use it positively to mean **not straight** or **not cisgender**, or simply to express that they don’t fit neatly into traditional labels; however, it _was_ historically used as a slur – so whether it’s appropriate depends on **who is using it and how**; when teens use it about themselves or within LGBTQ+ spaces, it’s usually affirming but when used _at_ someone in a mocking or hostile way, it can still be hurtful

**Slang words beginning with R**

**“Ratio”:** often used to explain the ratio between likes and comments; “She gets millions of views but only 10k likes, her ratio is a red flag”

**“Real”:** said to agree with someone; “What you said was so real”

**“Reckless”:** used positively when being “messy”, an aesthetic of being true to yourself; “I feel so reckless! I’m free!”

**“Reckon”:** used to ask for an opinion on something; “Whaddya reckon?”

**“Rent free”:** something/topic that takes over your mind for an allotted period of time; “Timothee Chalamet lives in my mind rent free”

**"Rizz":** short for charisma, the ability to charm or attract someone; “She has infinite rizz”

**"Roadman":** UK slang referring to someone who dresses in streetwear and engages in stereotypically urban behaviour; “He looks like a total roadman”

**Slang words beginning with S**

**“Salty”:** holding a little bit of remorse over a situation; “She's was so salty after I told her that her dog looks fat”

**“Sauce”:** when you get hung up on a topic, becoming out of touch with reality; “Lost in the sauce”

**“Serving”:** used to describe someone’s amazing outfit; “You are literally serving with that dress”

**“Sheesh”:** used when you're flabbergasted; “SHEESH!”

**“Ship”:** to couple up two people together who aren't actually together; “I ship them, they would look so good together”, "My friends ship me with him but I don't really like him"

**“Sic/Sick”:** something great, can be interchangeable with fire; “That is so sick”

**“Side eye”:** to judge someone’s comment or to explain someone was judging your; “Did you hear what she said...side eye”, "Did you see the side eye they gave me..."

**"Sigma":** refers to someone who’s independent, confident, and successful; "sigma rizz" = "you’ve got game"

**"Sigma" or "skibidi rizzler":** refers to someone who is popular or has charisma; “He is so sigma”

**“Simp”:** to demonstrate interest in someone in an obvious way, negative; “You are such a simp for Samantha”

**“Silent W”:** a silent win, not bragging about something positive that happened to you; “Me accidentally winning the raffle is such a Silent W”

**“Situationship”:** a one-sided relationship between two people or a relationship which is non-committal and confusing; “I'm stuck in a situationship”

**"Skibidi":** doesn’t actually mean anything, can mean something is “bad” or “cool” but it can also simply be used as a word or meme to confuse people or to start a joke; “You’re so skibidi”

**“Smol”:** diminutive of small, used to describe something as cute and tiny; “My cat is so smol”

**“Snatched”:** used to describe someone’s body or looks, “your waist is snatched”

**“Social battery”:** the amount of energy someone has to in social settings; “My social battery is running out, I gotta head home”

**"Slay":** used to describe something impressive or someone who performed very well; “Girl you slayed that presentation”
